title: Hollow Microneedle-based Sensor for Multiplexed Transdermal Electrochemical Sensing
protocol: Design a pyramidal-shaped hollow microneedle array using Solidworks software.
Create a support structure for the microneedle array using Magics RP software.
Upload the linked support and microneedle array files into Perfactory RP software.
Choose the number of microneedle arrays to be fabricated in Perfactory RP software.
Determine the placement of devices on the fabrication plate within the software.
Run calibration in ultraviolet mode at 180 mW for the Perfactory system.
Verify the deviation in energy during calibration is within ±2 mW.
Remove the completed microneedle arrays from the baseplate after fabrication.
Develop the microneedles in isopropanol for 15 minutes.
Dry the microneedle arrays with compressed air.
Cure the microneedles at room temperature for 50 seconds using the Otoflash Postcuring System.
Validate microneedle fabrication via microscopy.
Use a laser system to cut holes in a flat flexible cable to expose individual copper wires.
Place the flat flexible cables in an alignment jig on the laser ablation plate.
Create 500 μm diameter cavities in the insulating portion of the flexible cable using a rastering approach.
Clean the modified cables with acetone sprayed from an airbrush at 40 psi.
Rinse the cleaned cables with isopropanol and deionized water.
Verify under a microscope that no insulating film remains over exposed copper strips.
Ablate Melinex tape with the same pattern as the electrode strips, orienting it over the ablated electrode strips.
Compress the ablated Melinex tape onto the electrode strips at 3000 psi for 2 minutes.
Mix 10 mg of glucose oxidase and 2.2 mg of poly(ethylenimine) until a homogeneous mixture is obtained.
Add 60 mg of rhodium on carbon powder (5% loading) to the mixture and mix thoroughly.
Add 40 mg mineral oil and subsequently mix to form a homogenous paste.
Store the glucose sensitive carbon paste at 4°C until use, up to one week after preparation.
Mix 30% (w/w) mineral oil with 70% (w/w) graphite powder to obtain pH sensitive carbon paste.
Pack the prepared pastes into electrode cavities as described in section 3.4.
Make a solution of 10 mM Fast Blue RR diazonium salt in 0.5 M phosphoric acid.
Place a 20 μl drop of this solution over the packed paste electrode for 30 minutes to spontaneously chemisorb the Fast Blue PR diazonium salt.
Rinse with deionized water and store the electrode in buffer or deionized water when not in use.
Mix 2.5 mg of rhodium on carbon powder with 2.5 mg of lactate oxidase.
Alternate between sonication and vortexing for five rotations, each lasting 5 minutes.
Apply the respective pastes over the electrode cavities using a thin piece of plastic as a trowel.
Pack the paste until a smooth surface is achieved.
Remove excess paste with a second clean weighing boat.
Wash the packed paste with deionized water.
Measure the chronoamperometric response of the sensor at -0.15 V in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH=7.5).
Record the current after 15 seconds for lactate detection.
Measure the chronoamperometric response of the sensor at -0.05 V in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.0) for glucose detection.
Record the current after 15 seconds for glucose detection.
Monitor pH by running cyclic voltammetric scans from -0.7 V to 0.8 V at 100 mV/s and recording the position of the oxidative peak potential.
Create calibration curves for glucose and lactate sensors by successive additions of the respective analyte, followed by chronoamperometric measurements after each addition.
Perform fixed potential chronoamperometric measurements under stirring, allowing sufficient time (~10-100 seconds) between each analyte addition for current stabilization.
Create pH calibration curves by measuring the position of the oxidative peak potential over a series of known pH values from 5 to 8 in 1.0 pH unit increments and recording cyclic voltammograms.
Stir the solution briefly after each lactate addition when obtaining chronoamperometric curves for lactate detection.
Allow sufficient time for stabilization after each spike in concentration.
Measure the current response to determine the concentration of lactate in an unknown solution.
Monitor the increase in current upon increasing glucose concentration for standardization.
